episode_title: How AHMM Survived Its First Five Years | Simon Allford
question: How did AHMM survive its first five years as an architecture practice founded in 1986?
transcript_excerpt: Simon Allford founded AHMM with three colleagues in 1986 when all were just 27 years old and recently qualified. They lived hand-to-mouth for the first two years, working off debt and putting money on credit cards. The practice received consultancy work from other architects and benefited from the business advice of mentor Bill Jack. Allford emphasizes that surviving five years is critical because it takes five years to complete a building, which then becomes collateral to show the world as their own work.

episode_title: How AHMM Survived Its First Five Years | Simon Allford
question: What advice does Simon Allford give to architects starting their own practice?
transcript_excerpt: Allford advises new practice founders to keep super lean, not undervalue yourself, invest in time, and recognize it will be tough but enjoy it along the way. He stresses the importance of talking to peers at different career stages, being open and honest about struggles, and noting that the architecture community is generous and open. He emphasizes not putting on a show in interviews but instead being yourself, sharing work with brevity and elegance, and engaging in genuine conversation rather than laying out architectural theory.

episode_title: How AHMM Survived Its First Five Years | Simon Allford
question: What is AHMM's philosophy on making money versus making architecture?
transcript_excerpt: According to Allford, AHMM's core philosophy is that they make money to make architecture, with architecture as the primary driver. The more good architecture they make, the more money they earn to invest in more good architecture. Having money gives confidence to turn down the wrong job and to invest in competitions and people. This approach allows the practice to immerse itself in architectural culture and absorb the best of it.

episode_title: How AHMM Survived Its First Five Years | Simon Allford
question: How has architecture technology changed since AHMM was founded and what should architects know about AI and digital tools?
transcript_excerpt: When AHMM began in 1989, none of the founders could use a computer to make 3D drawings and only nerds used computers. The tools have evolved from pencils to quills to early computer models and now to 3D environments like Enscape. Allford advises that architects should be abreast of the technology of their time without obsessing over it, as it will not shape ability but only how they engage with architecture. He notes that while technology has increased productivity, expectations have increased but fees have not, and he values brainpower to make good decisions over excessive computer-generated options.

episode_title: How AHMM Survived Its First Five Years | Simon Allford
question: Why does Simon Allford believe five-year architecture degrees and two diplomas are not necessary?
transcript_excerpt: Allford argues that five-year degrees followed by a second diploma are too long and potentially unnecessary. He believes a three-year degree provides a foundation and introduction to architecture, and then the office should take responsibility for continuing development. He compares it to studying philosophy or history—a degree does not make you a philosopher or historian. He advocates for earn and learn courses and apprenticeships as more accessible pathways into architecture, noting that the government's decision to stop level six apprenticeships is counterproductive.
